screens.title: Scripting Physics Interactions: Triggers & Collisions
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we'll clarify the two ways Unity reports interactions: collisions and triggers. You will learn how Unity calls back into your C# code when objects hit each other physically, and how it reports overlaps when colliders are configured as triggers. Understanding this distinction matters because collisions provide rich impact data like contact points and relative velocity, while triggers are lightweight detectors that signal presence without a physical response. Both systems require at least one interacting object to have a Rigidbody, which is a frequent source of confusion. We'll also walk through practical scripts you can attach to objects, such as a coin that a player picks up using a trigger, and a destructible block that takes damage from impact forces. You'll see how to use CompareTag for efficient identity checks and how to access an object from the Collision or Collider parameter. By the end of this lesson you should be able to pick the right callback for your gameplay need, implement the correct signature in a MonoBehaviour, and avoid missing events due to Rigidbody or collider misconfiguration. Think about an in-game example you want to script: is it a physical hit or merely an overlap? That choice guides your implementation.

screens.title: Collision Events: what they are and when to use them
screens.narratorSegment: A collision event in Unity is a callback invoked when two colliders, neither marked as a trigger, contact each other and at least one has a Rigidbody. These callbacks are designed for interactions that imply a physical response: things should bounce, take damage, stop moving, or otherwise react under physics. The three primary methods are OnCollisionEnter, OnCollisionStay, and OnCollisionExit. OnCollisionEnter fires once on the first frame of contact, OnCollisionStay fires every physics update while the objects are touching, and OnCollisionExit fires when contact ends. Collision callbacks receive a Collision parameter which exposes detailed information such as the other GameObject, the specific Collider involved, contact points, and the relativeVelocity at the moment of impact. A common use-case is computing damage based on impact force: you can check collision. relativeVelocity. magnitude and compare it against a threshold. A common misconception is believing that two static colliders will trigger events: they will not. At least one collider must have a Rigidbody. Example: a projectile with a Rigidbody and a sphere collider hitting a destructible wall that has a collider and a Rigidbody will trigger OnCollisionEnter on the Rigidbody object. Key takeaway: use collision callbacks when you need physics context like contact normals or impact velocity, and remember to check Rigidbody setup before debugging missing events.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Collision Events
Collision Events
Definition and the Collision parameter.
When to use
For physical impacts where contact points, normals, or impact velocity matter for gameplay.
Key callbacks
OnCollisionEnter, OnCollisionStay, OnCollisionExit. Each receives a Collision argument with useful data.
Common misconception
Two static colliders will not produce collision callbacks. Ensure at least one collider has a Rigidbody.
Example use
Compute damage from impact using collision.relativeVelocity.magnitude and destroy or subtract health when a threshold is exceeded.
Key Takeaway

Collision callbacks provide physics context. Use them when impact details matter and ensure Rigidbody presence.

Collision parameter preview
The Collision object gives you access to the other object, the collider involved, contacts array, and relative velocity. Use these to compute impacts or query components on the other object.
Collision collision;
// Example properties you can use:
// collision.gameObject  -> the other GameObject
// collision.collider    -> the other Collider
// collision.contacts    -> contact points array
// collision.relativeVelocity -> impact velocity vector
Check your understanding
If your OnCollisionEnter never fires, inspect whether both colliders are static, or if colliders are marked Is Trigger by mistake.

screens.title: Collision callbacks: Enter, Stay, Exit
screens.narratorSegment: Unity calls three collision callbacks to report different phases of contact. OnCollisionEnter is invoked once when two non-trigger colliders first make contact; use it for one-off responses like playing a hit sound or applying immediate damage. OnCollisionStay runs each physics update while the objects remain in contact; this is useful for continuous effects, such as applying friction, gradual damage while a player is being crushed, or sustaining a collision-based force. OnCollisionExit triggers when the colliders separate; use it to stop continuous effects, reset state, or trigger events when contact ends. A common practical flow is computing impact damage on enter, and then applying a lingering knockback or ongoing damage during stay, finally resetting invulnerability or movement constraints on exit. Remember that these callbacks receive a Collision parameter, allowing you to check the other object's tag or components via collision. gameObject or collision. collider. GetComponent. A typical mistake is doing heavy work inside OnCollisionStay without guarding by time or thresholds; this can lead to repeated expensive operations. Instead, use short-circuit checks and keep per-frame work minimal. Now think of a collision sequence you need in your game: map enter to immediate reactions, stay to ongoing effects, and exit to cleanup and state reset.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Collision Callbacks Flow
Enter → Stay → Exit
Connect callbacks to gameplay phases and avoid heavy per-frame costs.
OnCollisionEnter
Triggered once on first contact. Use for sounds, single damage calculations, and impulse reactions.
OnCollisionStay
Runs each physics frame while contact persists. Useful for sustained damage, friction, or ongoing effects — keep work minimal.
OnCollisionExit
Called when objects separate. Use it to stop effects, reset timers, or mark interaction complete.
Concrete scenario
Imagine a rolling player that stomps on a fragile object: use OnCollisionEnter to check impact strength and subtract health. If the player remains pressing the object, OnCollisionStay can continue to apply pressure damage. OnCollisionExit then frees the object to recover or play a break animation.
Quick pitfalls
  • Don't perform expensive allocations inside OnCollisionStay.
  • Guard by time or thresholds if you need less frequent updates.
  • Confirm Rigidbody presence if callbacks never fire.

screens.title: Trigger Events: overlap detection without physical response
screens.narratorSegment: Trigger events occur when a collider marked with Is Trigger set to true overlaps another collider. Triggers do not block movement or produce a physical response; instead they report presence: OnTriggerEnter when an object first enters, OnTriggerStay while it remains inside, and OnTriggerExit when it leaves. The callback parameter is a Collider, not a Collision, because there are no contact points or relative velocities to report. Triggers are ideal for non-physical interactions: pickups, checkpoints, proximity-based dialogues, and zone-based effects. They are also lighter-weight than collision computations when you don't need physical response. A frequent setup is a collectible coin: the coin's collider is a trigger and the player has a Rigidbody. The coin's script checks other. CompareTag("Player"), accesses the player's component if needed, updates score, and destroys the coin. A common mistake is forgetting that one object still must have a Rigidbody; otherwise triggers will not fire. Another oversight is using triggers when you actually need impact data — for instance, damage from a high-speed impact should use collision callbacks because trigger events won't provide impact force. Choose triggers for detection, collisions for physics context.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Trigger Events
Trigger Events
Use triggers for detection zones and pickups where no physical response is required.
OnTriggerEnter
Called once when another collider enters the trigger volume.
OnTriggerStay
Called each physics frame while another collider remains inside the trigger.
OnTriggerExit
Called when a collider leaves the trigger volume.
Concrete example
A coin with a Sphere Collider set to Is Trigger detects when the player enters. The coin's script uses other.CompareTag("Player") to confirm identity, updates score, and destroys itself. The Collider parameter gives you the entering object's GameObject but not contact points or impact data.
Key Takeaway

Triggers are detectors. Use them for pickups and zones. Remember: at least one Rigidbody is still required.

screens.title: Collision vs Trigger: side-by-side
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the practical differences between collisions and triggers helps you choose the right tool. Collisions are for physical impacts: colliders not set as triggers collide and at least one object must have a Rigidbody. Collision callbacks provide a Collision parameter with contact points and relativeVelocity, which you can use to calculate damage, force, or to decide bounce direction. Triggers are for detection: colliders marked as Is Trigger report overlaps through a Collider parameter. Triggers do not provide contact data and do not apply forces. Use triggers for pickups, checkpoints, and environmental zones. Performance and intent also matter: triggers are conceptually lighter when you do not need physics resolution. A common error is using a trigger when you actually need impact force for damage; triggers cannot provide that. Another frequent issue is expecting callbacks on static colliders — Unity will not call OnCollisionEnter or OnTriggerEnter if both objects are static and neither has a Rigidbody. In practice, decide first whether you need physics detail. If yes, choose collision callbacks. If you only need to know presence, choose triggers and check tags with CompareTag to identify the entering or colliding object efficiently.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Collision vs Trigger
Collision (Non-trigger)
  • Provides Collision parameter with contact points and relativeVelocity.
  • Used for physical responses: bounce, damage from impact.
  • Requires at least one Rigidbody on the interacting pair.
Callbacks: OnCollisionEnter, OnCollisionStay, OnCollisionExit
Trigger (Is Trigger = true)

Callbacks: OnTriggerEnter, OnTriggerStay, OnTriggerExit
Practical selection guide
Ask: Do I need impact data or just detection? If impact data is required, use collision callbacks. If only presence is required, use triggers. Always confirm Rigidbody presence when events fail to fire.

screens.title: CoinCollector: a trigger-based pickup
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a simple coin pickup script that uses a trigger. The coin has a Sphere Collider with Is Trigger checked, and a Rigidbody that can be kinematic if you don't want it to be affected by gravity. The script registers OnTriggerEnter with a Collider parameter. Inside that method you first check whether the entering collider belongs to the player with CompareTag("Player"). This is efficient and avoids fragile string comparisons of object names. If the check passes, you can get a component such as a score manager on the player using other. GetComponent and update values safely after checking for null. Finally, call Destroy on the coin's GameObject to remove it from the scene. Important runtime considerations: ensure the player has a Rigidbody and a Collider, and that tags are set correctly. Also avoid heavy operations like allocations or expensive searches inside the callback. The visual code panel shows a minimal, clean implementation you can adapt: replace score updating with events, sound playback, or animation triggers. A common misconception is that a trigger needs both objects to be triggers — it does not; only the pick-up needs to be a trigger while the player typically has a normal collider and Rigidbody.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › CoinCollector.cs
Starter script (visual)
using UnityEngine;

public class CoinCollector : MonoBehaviour
{
    void OnTriggerEnter(Collider other)
    {
        if (other.CompareTag("Player"))
        {
            Debug.Log("Coin Collected by Player!");
            Destroy(gameObject); // Remove the coin
        }
    }
}
Notes: Use CompareTag for speed. If you need to update player state, call other.GetComponent<PlayerScoreManager>() after the tag check and guard against null.
Concrete adaptations
  • Play a pickup sound before destroying to guarantee audio feedback.
  • Use kinematic Rigidbody on coin if you move it via transform to avoid physics issues.
  • Emit an event instead of directly modifying player state for looser coupling.
Misconception check
Destroying the coin immediately is safe here, but if you need animation, consider disabling visuals and destroying after the animation completes instead of immediate Destroy to avoid missing effects.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › BlockDestroyer.cs
Starter script (visual)
using UnityEngine;

public class BlockDestroyer : MonoBehaviour
{
    public float health = 50f;
    public float damageThreshold = 5f; // Minimum relative velocity for damage

    void OnCollisionEnter(Collision collision)
    {
        if (collision.gameObject.CompareTag("Player"))
        {
            float impactForce = collision.relativeVelocity.magnitude;
            if (impactForce > damageThreshold)
            {
                health -= impactForce;
                Debug.Log($"Block hit by Player! Impact: {impactForce:F2}, Health: {health:F2}");

                if (health <= 0)
                {
                    Debug.Log("Block destroyed!");
                    Destroy(gameObject);
                }
            }
        }
    }
}
Notes: Adjust damageThreshold to tune sensitivity. Use kinematic Rigidbody on static blocks that still need to detect collisions.
Practical tips
  • Use relativeVelocity.magnitude for a simple impact measure.
  • Clamp or scale damage to keep gameplay balanced.
  • Destroy projectiles on impact if appropriate to avoid duplicate hits.
Misconception check

screens.title: Best practices & common mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: When scripting physics interactions, a few rules save hours of debugging. First, always verify the Rigidbody requirement: at least one interacting object must have a Rigidbody for both collision and trigger events. If an object should not be moved by physics but still listen for events, make its Rigidbody kinematic. Second, use CompareTag to identify objects instead of checking object names; it's faster and less brittle. Third, avoid heavy per-frame operations inside OnCollisionStay or OnTriggerStay. If you need periodic effects, throttle updates with a timer or apply effects based on accumulated time. Fourth, guard GetComponent calls by checking they are not null before using returned components to prevent runtime errors. Fifth, separate responsibilities: let triggers notify a manager or emit an event instead of tightly coupling pickup logic to the player object. Common mistakes include marking the wrong collider as a trigger, forgetting to set tags, or expecting trigger callbacks to include collision contact information. For performance, prefer simple boolean checks and cached component references rather than repeated lookups. These practices help keep your game stable, responsive, and easier to maintain.

screens.title: Design pattern: decoupling triggers from game state
screens.narratorSegment: When a trigger should change broader game state, avoid placing all logic inside the trigger script. Instead, use a decoupled approach: the trigger detects the player and either fires an event or calls a manager that owns score, inventory, or level state. This keeps individual object scripts small and focused and makes behavior reusable. For example, a coin's OnTriggerEnter checks other. CompareTag("Player") and then calls a ScoreManager. AddScore method or invokes an event that the ScoreManager subscribes to. This allows the coin to remain a simple emitter and the manager to control how the score is displayed, saved, or multiplied by modifiers. Decoupling also helps during testing: you can swap managers, disable score changes, or replay events without changing the pickup object. Another advantage is testability: manager methods can be unit tested independently from physics interactions. A common misconception is that direct component manipulation is always simpler. In small prototypes it may be, but as systems grow, decoupled event-driven design reduces coupling, surprises, and duplicated logic across many pickup objects. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we'll clarify the two ways Unity reports interactions: collisions and triggers. You will learn how Unity calls back into your C# code when objects hit each other physically, and how it reports overlaps when colliders are configured as triggers. Understanding this distinction matters because collisions provide rich impact data like contact points and relative velocity, while triggers are lightweight detectors that signal presence without a physical response. Both systems require at least one interacting object to have a Rigidbody, which is a frequent source of confusion. We'll also walk through practical scripts you can attach to objects, such as a coin that a player picks up using a trigger, and a destructible block that takes damage from impact forces. You'll see how to use CompareTag for efficient identity checks and how to access an object from the Collision or Collider parameter. By the end of this lesson you should be able to pick the right callback for your gameplay need, implement the correct signature in a MonoBehaviour, and avoid missing events due to Rigidbody or collider misconfiguration. Think about an in-game example you want to script: is it a physical hit or merely an overlap? That choice guides your implementation.

These objectives map to practical skills you'll need when scripting physics interactions in Unity. First, you will distinguish collision events from trigger events: collisions are physical impacts and provide contact data, while triggers detect overlaps without physical response. Second, you will implement standard C# callbacks such as the collision trio and the trigger trio so you can respond at the right moments. Third, you'll learn how to use the Collision and Collider parameters to access the other GameObject, read contact points, and compute things like impact force. Fourth, you'll apply best practices—ensuring a Rigidbody is present when needed, using CompareTag instead of fragile name checks, and deciding when to make a Rigidbody kinematic versus dynamic. Each objective combines a concrete coding ability and a reason why it matters for gameplay: correct events ensure pickups register, damage is applied reliably, and performance stays predictable. As you work through the examples, keep the Rigidbody rule in mind and practice explicit component checks to avoid silent bugs. These skills are directly applicable to common tasks like creating collectibles, pressure plates, and destructible obstacles.

These objectives translate into hands-on capabilities and quick debugging checks you will perform while building gameplay. You should be able to attach a script to a GameObject and implement the correct callback signature for collisions or triggers, and confirm events fire by using efficient checks such as CompareTag. You will know to verify Rigidbody presence: events only fire when one of the pair has a Rigidbody, so if nothing happens, check that first. You'll also know how to read the Collision parameter to get impact force or contact points, and how to use the Collider parameter to find the GameObject inside a trigger. These are practical, testable outcomes: create a collectible coin that disappears when the player enters its trigger, and make a destructible block that subtracts health when hit with sufficient relative velocity. Each objective has a verification step: run the scene, observe console logs, and confirm the event callbacks are called. A small checklist—tags set, Rigidbody present, collider configured as trigger or not—will save you debugging time. Practice these checks every time an event seems to fail.

A collision event in Unity is a callback invoked when two colliders, neither marked as a trigger, contact each other and at least one has a Rigidbody. These callbacks are designed for interactions that imply a physical response: things should bounce, take damage, stop moving, or otherwise react under physics. The three primary methods are OnCollisionEnter, OnCollisionStay, and OnCollisionExit. OnCollisionEnter fires once on the first frame of contact, OnCollisionStay fires every physics update while the objects are touching, and OnCollisionExit fires when contact ends. Collision callbacks receive a Collision parameter which exposes detailed information such as the other GameObject, the specific Collider involved, contact points, and the relativeVelocity at the moment of impact. A common use-case is computing damage based on impact force: you can check collision. relativeVelocity. magnitude and compare it against a threshold. A common misconception is believing that two static colliders will trigger events: they will not. At least one collider must have a Rigidbody. Example: a projectile with a Rigidbody and a sphere collider hitting a destructible wall that has a collider and a Rigidbody will trigger OnCollisionEnter on the Rigidbody object. Key takeaway: use collision callbacks when you need physics context like contact normals or impact velocity, and remember to check Rigidbody setup before debugging missing events.

Unity calls three collision callbacks to report different phases of contact. OnCollisionEnter is invoked once when two non-trigger colliders first make contact; use it for one-off responses like playing a hit sound or applying immediate damage. OnCollisionStay runs each physics update while the objects remain in contact; this is useful for continuous effects, such as applying friction, gradual damage while a player is being crushed, or sustaining a collision-based force. OnCollisionExit triggers when the colliders separate; use it to stop continuous effects, reset state, or trigger events when contact ends. A common practical flow is computing impact damage on enter, and then applying a lingering knockback or ongoing damage during stay, finally resetting invulnerability or movement constraints on exit. Remember that these callbacks receive a Collision parameter, allowing you to check the other object's tag or components via collision. gameObject or collision. collider. GetComponent. A typical mistake is doing heavy work inside OnCollisionStay without guarding by time or thresholds; this can lead to repeated expensive operations. Instead, use short-circuit checks and keep per-frame work minimal. Now think of a collision sequence you need in your game: map enter to immediate reactions, stay to ongoing effects, and exit to cleanup and state reset.

Trigger events occur when a collider marked with Is Trigger set to true overlaps another collider. Triggers do not block movement or produce a physical response; instead they report presence: OnTriggerEnter when an object first enters, OnTriggerStay while it remains inside, and OnTriggerExit when it leaves. The callback parameter is a Collider, not a Collision, because there are no contact points or relative velocities to report. Triggers are ideal for non-physical interactions: pickups, checkpoints, proximity-based dialogues, and zone-based effects. They are also lighter-weight than collision computations when you don't need physical response. A frequent setup is a collectible coin: the coin's collider is a trigger and the player has a Rigidbody. The coin's script checks other. CompareTag("Player"), accesses the player's component if needed, updates score, and destroys the coin. A common mistake is forgetting that one object still must have a Rigidbody; otherwise triggers will not fire. Another oversight is using triggers when you actually need impact data — for instance, damage from a high-speed impact should use collision callbacks because trigger events won't provide impact force. Choose triggers for detection, collisions for physics context.

Understanding the practical differences between collisions and triggers helps you choose the right tool. Collisions are for physical impacts: colliders not set as triggers collide and at least one object must have a Rigidbody. Collision callbacks provide a Collision parameter with contact points and relativeVelocity, which you can use to calculate damage, force, or to decide bounce direction. Triggers are for detection: colliders marked as Is Trigger report overlaps through a Collider parameter. Triggers do not provide contact data and do not apply forces. Use triggers for pickups, checkpoints, and environmental zones. Performance and intent also matter: triggers are conceptually lighter when you do not need physics resolution. A common error is using a trigger when you actually need impact force for damage; triggers cannot provide that. Another frequent issue is expecting callbacks on static colliders — Unity will not call OnCollisionEnter or OnTriggerEnter if both objects are static and neither has a Rigidbody. In practice, decide first whether you need physics detail. If yes, choose collision callbacks. If you only need to know presence, choose triggers and check tags with CompareTag to identify the entering or colliding object efficiently.

The coin has a Sphere Collider with Is Trigger checked, and a Rigidbody that can be kinematic if you don't want it to be affected by gravity. The script registers OnTriggerEnter with a Collider parameter. Inside that method you first check whether the entering collider belongs to the player with CompareTag("Player"). GetComponent and update values safely after checking for null. Finally, call Destroy on the coin's GameObject to remove it from the scene. A common misconception is that a trigger needs both objects to be triggers — it does not; only the pick-up needs to be a trigger while the player typically has a normal collider and Rigidbody.

A damageThreshold helps ignore light taps and prevents immediate breakage from minor contacts. Also, if your block should be static but still receive collision callbacks, give it a kinematic Rigidbody so Unity treats it as dynamic for event dispatch while keeping its world position fixed. When a trigger should change broader game state, avoid placing all logic inside the trigger script. Instead, use a decoupled approach: the trigger detects the player and either fires an event or calls a manager that owns score, inventory, or level state. This keeps individual object scripts small and focused and makes behavior reusable. For example, a coin's OnTriggerEnter checks other. CompareTag("Player") and then calls a ScoreManager. AddScore method or invokes an event that the ScoreManager subscribes to. This allows the coin to remain a simple emitter and the manager to control how the score is displayed, saved, or multiplied by modifiers. Decoupling also helps during testing: you can swap managers, disable score changes, or replay events without changing the pickup object. Another advantage is testability: manager methods can be unit tested independently from physics interactions. A common misconception is that direct component manipulation is always simpler. In small prototypes it may be, but as systems grow, decoupled event-driven design reduces coupling, surprises, and duplicated logic across many pickup objects. Let's summarize three essential concepts. First, collisions are physical interactions between non-trigger colliders and provide a Collision object with contact points and relative velocity; use them when impact details matter. Second, triggers are overlap detectors that report presence through a Collider parameter without a physical response; use them for pickups, zones, and sensors. Third, the Rigidbody requirement is fundamental: at least one interacting object must have a Rigidbody for collisions or triggers to fire. Remember also to use CompareTag for identity checks, cache component references to reduce overhead, and decouple pickup logic from game state by using managers or events.
